speaker_role: current admissions officers (Liz Kinsley, Director of Admission, Northwestern; Robert Ellis, Associate Director of Undergraduate Admission, Northwestern)
commercial_incentive: None - official Northwestern University admissions office content, no products or services promoted
key_insights: Readers primarily look in recommendations for how a student will contribute to the classroom/learning community: collaboration, how they handle adversity, willingness to ask for help - qualities students often can't credibly claim about themselves

Qualitative and 'relative' language (how a student compares to others in that teacher's career, not just that class) is especially valuable; grids/rating scales on recommendation forms are read and can highlight outlier strengths, but their absence isn't penalized

Bullet points are explicitly fine and preferred by both speakers over long prose ('we're both team bullets'); brevity doesn't compromise substance, and readers process 51,000+ applications/year so efficiency helps

Advises students to ask a junior-year teacher (who has known them across a full year) rather than defaulting to senior-year teachers, who may only know the student 2-3 months by application time; the subject doesn't have to match intended major - an English teacher's insight into an aspiring engineer's classroom presence can be equally valuable

Best practice is asking by the end of junior year to give teachers time; students should track school-specific requirements (e.g., some require a math + humanities teacher) to avoid asking teachers unnecessarily

Recommenders should avoid copy-pasted 'superlative' language, since Northwestern often reads multiple applications from the same high school and reused generic praise ('most rare intellect') dilutes impact - though reused factual/curricular paragraphs (e.g., describing standard AP US History content) are expected and fine

Cites average U.S. college counselor caseload around 400 students, explaining why admissions readers don't penalize thin or templated counselor letters and will not hold pandemic-related context (reduced teacher-student contact) against a student

Supplemental recommendation letters (e.g., from a coach, pastor, or research mentor) are valuable only if they add genuinely new information not already covered elsewhere in the application; otherwise they can bloat the file without helping
specific_numbers_or_facts: Northwestern received over 51,000 applications in the cited year
Average U.S. college counselor caseload cited as roughly 400 students
Northwestern requires at least one teacher recommendation from an academic subject (most often sees two) plus one counselor/administrator recommendation
notable_or_distinctive: Rare direct-from-admissions-officer detail on exactly how 'relative' language and rating grids are used to calibrate a student's standing within their own school/classroom context, and explicit confirmation that bullet-point letters are preferred over prose.
reliability_notes: Reflects one institution's (Northwestern's) stated practices as of this video's publication (~2021 per manifest); other schools' committees may weigh recommendation letters differently, though much of the general guidance (junior-year teacher, avoid generic superlatives) is broadly applicable and credibly sourced from named current admissions staff.
